messages.author: f8a4136bfeaed71c
messages.subject: Problem with missing covariates
parts:
Hi all,

I am running to see how I can apply Stan for a sequence of models. I have a response Y, regressing on X (X is binary) and X has some missing values. Because of that, X is regressing on Z to impute missing values. The model part is as follows:

model{
vector[N] mu1;
vector[N] mu2;
int X_bin[N];

for (i in 1 : N){
    mu1[i] = betaX * Z[i];

X[i] ~ normal(mu1[i], 1);

if (X[i] >= cpX) {X_bin[i] = 1;} else {X_bin[i] = 0;} 

    mu2[i] = betaY[1] + betaY[2] * X_bin[i];

Y[i] ~ normal(mu2[i], sigma);
}
}

It seems the codes is easy to understand. In the code, X_bin is binary whereas X is a latent normal combine with a cutpoint (to overcome the problem of cannot defining discrete variables in parameter blocks).

However, models does not converge after 5000 iterations (n_eff is very small and Rhat is very high).

Do you know why is the reason?

Kind regards,
Tran.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts: The problem is in this statement,

which branches on the value of a parameter cpX. By the way,
that could've been written more simply as:

X_bin = X[i] >= cpX;

The problem is that the branching on the parameter breaks
differentiability of the log density through X_bin and
down to cpX.

What you want to do is marginalize out the value of X_bin[i]
if this is the model you want to code.

- Bob

messages.author: f8a4136bfeaed71c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts:
Hi,

I cannot here marginalize because the idea is obtaining a value for X (here means X_bin) to plug into the regression model of Y on X_bin. Without this, the model cannot run because of NaN values for the location of y ~normal(...X, sigma). So I really want to have imputed values for X (from X regressing on Z) to help build model for Y.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts:
You can do both the regression and the imputation by marginalizing
out. In each case of the marginalization, you'll know X_bin. And
you can estimate the probability of each X_bin value conditioned on
the data by normalizing the density contributions for all of X_bin's
values. Then you can make draws of X_bin in generated quantities if
you really want a sample as opposed to directly calculating most
expectations of interest.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts:
You shouldn't need to use the missing variables in the model block.
If you think you need to model the missing data as parameters so
that you can use those parameters in inference, you don't need them.
Imputing the missing values then using them in the fit won't change
the fit. (Sometimes they can in semi-supervised learning problems
where the outcome is missing but the covariates are observed.)

Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters, so there's no way to
generate them in the model block without really ugly and inefficient
hacks that we very strongly discourage.

- Bob

messages.author: f8a4136bfeaed71c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts:
Hi Bob,

I have the filling that imputing the missing values and using them in one program might not change the fit. However, consider the following artificial data set:

X1 X2 X3 Y
1 NA 0 4
2 NA 1 5
3 NA 1 7
4 1 NA 5
5 0 NA 5
6 0 NA 4

If we want to regress Y on X2 and X3 (binary variable) and if we do not do any thing for X2 and X3 then we have nothing to do because in all case either X2 or X3 are missing.

Of course in a real dataset that kind of missingness might not be happen but if we discard cases with missing values then we lose a lot of observations.

That is why I really want that Stan can help me to impute (or generate) and the re-use the imputed values in the regression model.

For continuous variables everything is OK because I can specify the missing values as parameters. Unfortunately, I have to work with binary data.

Kind regards,
Tran.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
parts:
If you have to impute discrete data, then you
can often do it one observation at a time, in
which case the marginalization will be tractable.

You'll need to provide a probability model
for log p(X1, X2, X3, Y) and presumably that's just

SUM_n log p(X1[n], X2[n], X3[n], Y[n])

Then marginalize out the necessary X's on the inside.

- Bob
